88780.e: Augusta Raurica was a Roman town on the Rhine. The Romans built roads, temples and houses there.
88780.m: Augusta Raurica is an old Roman town.

88781.q: Near which place is Augusta Raurica today?
88781.e: The remains of the Roman town are in Augst in the canton of Basel-Landschaft and in Kaiseraugst in the canton of Aargau. The site is on the Rhine near Basel.
88781.m: Augusta Raurica is in Augst near Basel.

88782.q: Which large building can you still see in Augusta Raurica?
88782.e: The Roman theatre is very well preserved. Today, performances take place there again in summer.
88782.m: There is an old Roman theatre in Augusta Raurica.

88783.q: Which festival takes place in Augusta Raurica every year?
88783.e: At the Roman Festival, people in Roman clothes show how life used to be. There are markets, games and shows.
88783.m: A Roman Festival is held in Augusta Raurica every year.

88784.q: What can you see in the rebuilt Roman house in Augusta Raurica?
88784.e: The Roman house is furnished with a kitchen, a workshop and furniture. That way you can see how a Roman family lived.
88784.m: The Roman house shows how the Romans lived.

88785.q: Which language did the Romans in Augusta Raurica speak?
88785.e: The Romans spoke Latin. That is why the inscriptions on stones in Augusta Raurica are in Latin.

88786.q: Roughly how long ago was Augusta Raurica founded?
88786.e: The founding of Augusta Raurica is dated to the year 44 BC. That is more than 2,000 years ago.
88786.m: Augusta Raurica is over 2,000 years old.

88787.q: What did Stone Age people mainly paint on cave walls?
88787.e: In the cave paintings you can see horses, bison, deer and mammoths. These were animals the people knew and hunted.
88787.m: Stone Age people mainly painted animals.

88788.q: What did Stone Age people use to paint in the caves?
88788.e: Red and yellow paints were made from coloured earth, and black from charcoal. People painted with their fingers, moss or brushes made of hair.
88788.m: Cave painters used colours from earth and charcoal.

88789.q: Who discovered the Lascaux cave in 1940?
88789.e: Four teenagers found the cave by chance when they followed a hole in the ground. Inside they discovered the paintings.

88790.q: Which pictures did Stone Age people make on cave walls with their hands?
88790.e: They put their hand on the wall and blew paint around it. This left the outline of the hand.
88790.m: There are also handprints in caves.

88791.q: How did the cave painters get light in the dark cave?
a: Through holes in the cave roof
88791.e: It was pitch dark in the caves. People used torches and lamps in which animal fat burned.

88792.q: Roughly how old are the oldest cave paintings in Europe?
88792.e: The paintings in the Chauvet Cave in France, for example, are more than 30,000 years old. At that time mammoths still lived in Europe.
88792.m: Some cave paintings are over 30,000 years old.

88793.q: In which country is the Altamira cave with its paintings of bison?
88793.e: The Altamira cave is in northern Spain. Its colourful bison are world-famous.
88793.m: The Altamira cave is in Spain.

88794.q: In Switzerland, who owns valuable old finds from the ground, such as Roman coins?
88794.e: According to the Civil Code, antiquities of scientific value belong to the canton in which they were found. But the finder is entitled to a fair reward.
88794.m: In Switzerland, valuable old finds belong to the canton.

88795.q: What should you do if you discover an old find in the ground?
88795.e: Finds must be reported. Experts can then study the site.
88795.m: Report old finds to the cantonal archaeology service.

88796.q: What did building workers find in Kaiseraugst in the winter of 1961/62?
88796.e: While digging for a sports ground, over 250 pieces of silver from Roman times came to light, including plates, spoons and coins. It is one of the largest silver treasures of late antiquity.
88796.m: A large Roman silver treasure was found in Kaiseraugst.

88797.q: What is found especially often in old treasure hoards?
88797.e: In the past, people often hid their money in pots in the ground. Coins last a long time, while wood, paper and cloth rot away in the earth.
88797.m: Many old treasures are made up of coins.

88798.q: Why did people in the past hide treasure in the ground?
88798.e: There were no banks like today. In dangerous times, people buried their valuables.
88798.m: In the past, people hid valuables in the ground.

88799.q: What did building workers find in Erstfeld in the canton of Uri in 1962?
88799.e: During building work in Erstfeld in 1962, seven golden Celtic neck rings and arm rings came to light. They are over 2000 years old.
88799.m: Celtic gold jewellery was found in Erstfeld.

88800.q: Why does a gold treasure not rust in the ground?
88800.e: Gold hardly reacts with water and air. That is why it still shines even after thousands of years.
88800.m: Gold stays shiny in the ground.

88801.q: What do you need in many cantons to search with a metal detector?
88801.e: Anyone who digs without permission can destroy archaeological sites. That is why many cantons require a permit.
88801.m: You often need permission to search with a metal detector.

88802.q: What did the ancient Egyptians wrap their mummies in?
88802.e: The body was wrapped in many metres of linen bandages. Small lucky charms were often placed between the bandages.
88802.m: Egyptian mummies are wrapped in linen.

88803.q: Which salt did the Egyptians use to dry out the body?
88803.e: The body was covered with natron for many days. The salt drew the water out.

88804.q: Why did the ancient Egyptians make mummies?
a: As a gift for the Nile
So that robbers would not find them
88804.e: The Egyptians believed the body had to be preserved for life in the afterlife. That is why they preserved it.
88804.m: Mummies were meant to preserve the body for the afterlife.

88805.q: What is the large stone coffin that some mummies lay in called?
88805.e: A sarcophagus is a large coffin made of stone. Inside it there were often wooden coffins with the mummy.
88805.m: A sarcophagus is a stone coffin.

88806.q: Which animals did the ancient Egyptians also turn into mummies?
88806.e: Cats were sacred animals in Egypt. Thousands of cat mummies have been found.

88807.q: Roughly how long did mummification take in Egypt?
88807.e: Drying, anointing and wrapping took a lot of time. Altogether it took about 70 days.

88808.q: How can a mummy also form completely naturally?
88808.e: In ice, dry desert sand or bogs, a body hardly decays. This is how mummies form without human help.
88808.m: Ice and dryness can create mummies.

88809.q: What other nickname does Ötzi have?
88809.e: Because he lay in glacier ice, Ötzi is also called the Iceman. His name comes from the Ötztal Alps.
88809.m: Ötzi is also called the Iceman.

88810.q: On which great river are the pyramids of Giza?
88810.e: The pyramids stand on the west bank of the Nile. Stones for building them were also transported on the river.
88810.m: The pyramids of Giza are by the Nile.

88811.q: What were the Roman public baths called, whose remains can be found in Augusta Raurica?
88811.e: The thermae had warm and cold pools. The Romans met there to bathe and chat.

88812.q: How do archaeologists study sites that lie underwater in a lake?
88812.e: Underwater archaeologists dive into lakes with special equipment. In this way they explore, for example, the remains of old villages on the lake bed.

88813.q: Which organ fills with air when you breathe in?
88813.e: When you breathe in, air flows into the lungs. There the body takes what it needs to live.
88813.m: When you breathe in, your lungs fill with air.

88814.q: Which muscle under the lungs helps most with breathing in?
88814.e: The diaphragm is a flat muscle under the lungs. When it tightens, space is made and air flows in.
88814.m: The diaphragm is our most important breathing muscle.

88815.q: Where in the body are the lungs?
88815.e: The lungs fill almost the whole chest. The ribs protect them on all sides.
88815.m: The lungs are in the chest.

88816.q: Why is the left lung slightly smaller than the right?
88816.e: The heart lies a little more on the left side of the chest. That is why the left lung is a bit smaller.
88816.m: The heart needs room next to the left lung.

88817.q: Where does the air you breathe in end up in the end?
a: In the air sacs of the lungs
88817.e: The air travels through finer and finer tubes into tiny air sacs. There the body takes in the oxygen.
88817.m: The air ends up in the tiny air sacs.

88818.q: Through which openings of the body can we breathe in?
88818.e: Air enters the body through the nose or the mouth. The ears and eyes are not connected to the lungs.
88818.m: We breathe in through the nose or the mouth.

88819.q: What do you feel when you put your hand on your tummy and breathe in deeply?
88819.e: When you breathe in deeply, the diaphragm moves down and pushes the organs in your belly downwards. That is why your tummy pushes forward.
88819.m: When you breathe in deeply, your tummy pushes forward.

88820.q: What can you do if you breathe out with pursed lips?
88820.e: When you whistle, the air you breathe out flows through the small gap between your lips. This makes a high sound.
88820.m: With pursed lips and breath you can whistle.

88821.q: What happens to your tummy when you breathe out calmly?
88821.e: When you breathe in, your tummy pushes out a little. When you breathe out, the air flows out and your tummy gets flatter again.
88821.m: When you breathe out, your tummy gets flatter again.

88822.q: Why can you see your breath outdoors in winter?
a: Water in your breath forms droplets
It is smoke from your lungs
It is dust from your nose
88822.e: Our breath contains invisible water vapour. In cold air it cools down and turns into tiny droplets, which you see as little clouds.
88822.m: In the cold, the water in your breath becomes visible as little clouds.

88823.q: How does your breath feel when you breathe onto your hand?
88823.e: The air is warmed up inside our body. That is why the air we breathe out is warm.
88823.m: The air you breathe out is warm.

88824.q: What can you blow up with the air you breathe out?
88824.e: A balloon is made of stretchy rubber. When we blow air into it, it gets bigger.
88824.m: You can blow up a balloon with the air you breathe out.

88825.q: What makes a toy windmill spin when there is no wind outside?
88825.e: When you blow, the air you breathe out flows against the sails. The windmill spins as if in the wind.
88825.m: Blowing hard makes a toy windmill spin.

88826.q: What else do we need the air we breathe out for?
88826.e: When we speak, air from the lungs flows past the vocal cords. This makes sounds.
88826.m: We need the air we breathe out to speak.

88827.q: What makes a recorder play a note?
88827.e: When you play the recorder, you blow air into it. The air starts to vibrate and a note is made.
88827.m: A recorder sounds because air is blown into it.

88828.q: What do you blow out on a birthday cake?
88828.e: Candles need air to burn. A strong puff of air from your mouth blows out the little flame.
88828.m: You blow out birthday candles with the air you breathe out.

88829.e: The windpipe is a tube from the neck down into the chest. It carries air to the lungs.
88829.m: The windpipe carries air to the lungs.

88830.e: The windpipe contains lots of rings of cartilage. They make sure the tube does not collapse.
88830.m: Rings of cartilage keep the windpipe open.

88831.q: Where can you feel your windpipe?
a: At the front of your neck
At the back of your neck
88831.e: The windpipe lies at the front of the neck below the voice box. You can feel the firm rings there with your fingers.
88831.m: You can feel the windpipe at the front of your neck.

88832.q: What closes off the windpipe when we swallow?
88832.e: The epiglottis is a small flap. When we swallow, it covers the entrance to the windpipe so that no food gets in.
88832.m: The epiglottis protects the windpipe when we swallow.

88833.q: What are the airways in the lungs, which branch into finer and finer tubes, compared with?
88833.e: The windpipe is like a trunk, and the branches get finer and finer. That is why people speak of the bronchial tree.
88833.m: The airways in the lungs branch like a tree.

88834.q: How many branches does the windpipe divide into at the bottom?
88834.e: At the bottom the windpipe divides into two main branches, the bronchi. One goes to the right lung and one to the left lung.
88834.m: At the bottom the windpipe divides into two bronchi.

88835.q: Roughly how long is an adult's windpipe?
88835.e: In adults the windpipe is about 10 to 12 centimetres long. That is about as long as a ballpoint pen without its cap.
88835.m: An adult's windpipe is about 11 centimetres long.

88836.q: What do the tiny hairs inside the windpipe do?
88836.e: The inside of the windpipe is covered with mucus and tiny hairs called cilia. They move dust and dirt upwards and out of the lungs.

88837.q: What do the airways often make more of when you have a cold?
88837.e: When you have a cold, the airways are inflamed. They then make more mucus than usual.
88837.m: When you have a cold, the airways make more mucus.

88838.q: What happens to your sense of smell when you have a bad cold?
88838.e: With a cold, the nose is blocked and swollen. Smells hardly reach the cells that detect them.
88838.m: With a bad cold you smell less well.

88840.q: What does the nose do with very dry air?
88840.e: The lining of the nose is moist. As the air flows through, it picks up moisture, which is gentler on the lungs.
88840.m: The nose moistens the air we breathe.

88841.q: What does the nose make to trap dirt?
88841.e: A little mucus is constantly made in the nose. Dust and germs stick to it.
88841.m: Mucus in the nose traps dirt and germs.

88842.e: In the middle of the nose there is a thin wall of cartilage and bone. It is called the nasal septum.
88842.m: The nasal septum separates the two nostrils.

88843.q: Why do we often breathe through our mouth when we have a cold?
88843.e: With a cold, the lining of the nose swells and there is a lot of mucus. Then hardly any air gets through the nose.
88843.m: With a blocked nose we breathe through the mouth.

88844.q: What do we do to clear mucus out of the nose?
88844.e: When you blow your nose, you push air hard through it into a tissue. That way the mucus comes out.
88844.m: We clear mucus by blowing our nose.

88845.q: What can the nose do at the same time as breathing in?
88845.e: At the top of the nose there are smell cells. Smells reach them with the air we breathe in.
88845.m: We smell with our nose as we breathe in.

88846.e: When you cough, air is pushed out with great force. That gets crumbs and irritants out of the airways.

88847.q: What does the nose do all by itself when dust tickles it?
88847.e: When you sneeze, air is pushed hard through the nose and mouth. That blows the dust back out.
88847.m: Sneezing gets dust out of the nose.

88848.q: What do you call a movement the body makes all by itself, like coughing?
88848.e: A reflex happens automatically, without you having to think. Coughing, sneezing and blinking are reflexes.
88848.m: Coughing is a reflex of the body.

88849.q: What should you do if you have coughed into your hands?
88849.e: When you cough, germs get onto your hands. Soap and water wash them away.
88849.m: If you cough into your hands, wash them.

88850.q: With which illness do you often cough?
88850.e: With a cold, the airways are irritated. The body often reacts by coughing.
88850.m: You often cough when you have a cold.

88851.q: What often helps when your throat feels scratchy from coughing?
88851.e: Drinking keeps the throat moist and can ease the scratchiness. Warm tea is often drunk for this.
88851.m: Drinking plenty is good for a scratchy throat.

88852.q: What can set off a cough?
88852.e: Smoke irritates the airways. The body tries to get rid of the irritants by coughing.
88852.m: Smoke irritates the airways and causes coughing.

88853.q: Why should you keep your distance from others when you cough?
88853.e: When you cough, tiny droplets with germs fly through the air. If you keep your distance, others are less likely to catch it.
88853.m: Keeping your distance protects others from germs when you cough.

88854.q: Which muscle twitches when you have hiccups?
88854.e: When you have hiccups, the diaphragm keeps tightening suddenly. This makes you breathe in all at once.
88854.m: The diaphragm twitches when you have hiccups.

88855.q: What sound do you make when you have hiccups?
88855.e: With hiccups you suddenly breathe in and your throat closes straight away. This makes the typical “hic”.

88856.e: If you eat in a hurry or drink a lot of fizzy drinks, you can easily get hiccups. The full stomach then irritates the diaphragm.
88856.m: Eating too fast can cause hiccups.

88857.e: Hiccups are almost always harmless. Only if they last a very long time should you see a doctor.

88859.q: How long do ordinary hiccups usually last?
88859.e: Normal hiccups usually stop by themselves after a short time. Very long-lasting hiccups are rare.
88859.m: Hiccups usually stop after a short time.

88860.q: Which home remedy do many people try for hiccups?
a: Holding their breath for a moment
88860.e: Many people hold their breath for a moment or slowly drink a glass of water. But it has not been clearly proved that this really helps.
88860.m: Many people hold their breath for a moment to stop hiccups.

88861.q: Why do you have to breathe again after holding your breath for a while?
88861.e: Without breathing, the body soon runs short of fresh oxygen and used air builds up. Then you feel a strong urge to breathe.
88861.m: The body regularly needs fresh oxygen.

88862.q: When do we often hold our breath?
88862.e: We cannot breathe underwater. That is why we hold our breath when we dive.
88862.m: We hold our breath when diving.

88863.q: Which animal can hold its breath for a very long time?
88863.e: Sperm whales dive very deep for food. They can stay underwater for over an hour.
88863.m: The sperm whale can hold its breath for a very long time.

88864.q: What do you use to breathe just below the surface of the water without coming up?
88864.e: A snorkel is a tube that sticks up above the surface of the water. That way you can keep breathing with your face in the water.
88864.m: With a snorkel you can keep breathing in the water.

88865.q: What is diving with just a held breath, without a tank, called?
88865.e: In freediving you don't take an air tank. You dive with just one breath in your lungs.
88865.m: Freedivers dive with just a held breath.

88866.q: Where do scuba divers get air from underwater?
88866.e: Scuba divers carry a tank of compressed air on their back. They breathe from it through a hose.
88866.m: Scuba divers breathe air from a tank.

88867.q: Where is a whale's breathing hole?
88867.e: Whales breathe through a blowhole on top of their head. That way they can breathe without coming all the way out of the water.
88867.m: Whales breathe through a hole on top of their head.

88868.q: What do you usually do after holding your breath for a long time?
88868.e: After holding your breath, the body quickly needs fresh air. That is why you breathe in deeply and fast.
88868.m: After holding your breath you take a deep breath.

88869.q: Why does a dog pant on hot days?
88869.e: Dogs can hardly sweat. By panting they give off heat and cool themselves down.

88870.q: Where does a dog have sweat glands?
88870.e: Dogs only have a few sweat glands, mainly on the pads of their paws. That is not enough to cool down.
88870.m: Dogs sweat mainly through their paws.

88871.q: What does a panting dog stick far out?
88871.e: When a dog pants, its tongue hangs out of its mouth. A lot of heat is lost through the moist tongue.
88871.m: A panting dog sticks its tongue out.

88872.q: What cools a dog when it pants?
88872.e: When a dog pants, moisture evaporates on its tongue and in its airways. Evaporation takes heat away.
88872.m: Evaporating moisture cools a panting dog.

88873.q: How does a panting dog breathe?
88873.e: When panting, a dog breathes very fast and shallowly. That way lots of air flows over its moist tongue.

88874.q: Which pet sometimes pants too after playing wildly?
88874.e: Besides dogs, other mammals pant too, for example cats after a lot of effort. Fish, snails and worms cannot pant.
88874.m: Cats sometimes pant too after playing wildly.

88875.q: What does a panting dog definitely need on hot days?
88875.e: A dog loses water when it pants. Fresh water and a shady spot help it cope with the heat.
88875.m: Dogs need water and shade on hot days.

88876.q: Where must you never leave a dog on hot days?
88876.e: A closed car heats up very quickly in the sun. A dog cannot cool down enough there, even by panting.
88876.m: Never leave a dog in a hot car.

88877.q: Why does a soap bubble slowly sink to the ground after a while?
a: Its soapy skin is a little heavy
88877.e: There is only air inside, but the skin of soapy water weighs a little. That is why the bubble slowly sinks.
88877.m: The soapy skin makes a soap bubble slowly sink.

88878.q: What forms when two soap bubbles bump into each other and stick together?
88878.e: Two soap bubbles that touch share a flat wall. This makes a double bubble.
88878.m: Soap bubbles that stick together share a wall.

88879.q: What do you usually blow soap bubbles with?
88879.e: A thin skin of soapy water forms in the ring. When you blow through it, it bulges out into a bubble.
88879.m: You blow soap bubbles through a small ring.

88880.q: How do you blow a really big soap bubble?
88880.e: If you blow gently and steadily, the soapy skin can stretch slowly. Blowing hard makes lots of small bubbles.
88880.m: Big soap bubbles are blown slowly and steadily.

88881.q: In which weather do soap bubbles last longer outdoors?
88881.e: In damp air the soapy skin dries out less quickly. That is why the bubbles last longer.
88881.m: Soap bubbles last longer when the air is damp.

88882.q: What can you often see, small and curved, on a soap bubble?
88882.e: The smooth surface of a soap bubble reflects like a little glass ball. You can see the room or the sky in it, all distorted.

88883.q: What do you call a heap of lots and lots of tiny soap bubbles?
88883.e: Foam is made of countless tiny bubbles stuck together. You see it in the bath, for example.
88883.m: Foam is made of lots of small soap bubbles.

88884.q: What happens if soapy water gets in your eyes?
88884.e: Soap irritates the sensitive eyes. It is best to rinse them with clear water.
88884.m: Soapy water stings in your eyes.

88885.q: Roughly how many times a minute does an adult breathe at rest?
88885.e: An adult at rest breathes about 12 to 18 times a minute. When working hard, it is more.
88885.m: An adult at rest breathes about 15 times a minute.

88886.q: Do children breathe faster or slower than adults?
88886.e: Children have smaller lungs. That is why they breathe more times a minute than adults.

88887.e: When you run, your muscles work hard and need more oxygen. That is why you breathe faster and deeper.
88887.m: You breathe faster when you work hard.

88888.q: Roughly how much air does an adult breathe in with one calm breath?
88888.e: With one calm breath, about half a litre of air flows into the lungs. With a deep breath it is much more.
88888.m: A calm breath is about half a litre of air.

88889.q: Do we breathe when we are asleep?
88889.e: The brain controls breathing automatically. That is why we also breathe in our sleep without thinking about it.
88889.m: We breathe all by ourselves when we sleep.

88890.q: What does one whole breath consist of?
88890.e: A breath starts with breathing in and ends with breathing out. Then the next one begins.
88890.m: A breath consists of breathing in and breathing out.

88891.q: Roughly how many breaths does an adult take in a day?
88891.e: Because we breathe day and night without a break, we take over 20,000 breaths every day.
88891.m: A person breathes over 20,000 times every day.

88892.e: When you sigh, you breathe in especially deeply and breathe out so it can be heard. It often happens all by itself.
88892.m: A sigh is an especially deep breath.

88893.q: Why do pot plants sometimes die if you water them far too much?
88893.e: Roots also need oxygen from tiny air spaces in the soil. If the soil is always under water, they don't get this air.
88893.m: Plant roots also need air in the soil.

88894.e: Green plants and algae make oxygen using sunlight. They release it into the air and water.

88895.q: What bubbles in an aquarium so that the fish have enough oxygen?
88895.e: An air pump blows small bubbles into the water. This puts more oxygen into the water.
88895.m: An air pump brings oxygen into the aquarium.

88896.q: Why do fish in a warm pond sometimes gulp for air at the surface?
a: The water is short of oxygen
88896.e: Warm water can hold less oxygen than cold water. When oxygen is short, fish gulp for air at the top.

88897.q: What does a small device clipped onto your finger in hospital measure?
88897.e: The device shines light through the finger. That way it can tell how much oxygen the blood is carrying.
88897.m: A finger clip measures the oxygen in the blood.

88898.q: Which letter is used for oxygen in chemistry?
88898.e: The symbol O comes from the Latin name “oxygenium”. This is how oxygen is written in chemistry.

88899.q: What happens to a cut apple that is left in the air for a long time?
88899.e: Substances in the apple react with the oxygen in the air. This makes the cut surface turn brown.
88899.m: A cut apple turns brown in the air.

88900.q: What colour is the oxygen in the air?
88900.e: Oxygen is a gas with no colour and no smell. That is why we cannot see it.

88901.q: How much carbon dioxide does the air contain?
88901.e: Only a tiny part of the air is carbon dioxide, less than one thousandth. Even so, it matters for plants and for the climate.
88901.m: The air contains only very little carbon dioxide.

88902.q: Roughly how much of the air is oxygen?
88902.e: Oxygen makes up about 21 out of 100 parts of the air. That is roughly a fifth.
88902.m: About a fifth of the air is oxygen.

88903.q: How can you tell outdoors that the air is moving?
88903.e: We call moving air wind. We feel it on our skin and see the leaves move.
88903.m: We feel moving air as wind.

88904.q: What makes the air in a stuffy room fresh again?
88904.e: When you air a room, fresh air flows in from outside. The stale air goes out.
88904.m: Airing a room brings in fresh air.

88905.q: What pollutes the air we breathe in towns and cities?
88905.e: Cars, heating systems and factories give off exhaust fumes into the air. These can irritate the airways.
88905.m: Exhaust fumes pollute the air we breathe.

88906.q: Is there still oxygen in the air we breathe out?
88906.e: Breathed-out air still contains about 16 out of 100 parts oxygen. That is why rescue breaths can help another person.
88906.m: Even breathed-out air still contains oxygen.

88907.q: Where is the air usually cleaner?
88907.e: No cars drive in the woods and the trees filter dust out of the air. That is why the air there is usually cleaner.
88907.m: The air in the woods is usually clean.

88908.q: What does cigarette smoke do to the lungs?
88908.e: Smoke contains many poisonous substances. They settle in the lungs and can make them ill.

88909.q: In winter the air indoors is often very dry. Which device helps with this?
88909.e: A humidifier releases water into the air as a fine mist or steam. This helps against very dry air from the heating.
88909.m: A humidifier makes dry air moister.

88910.q: Why is ice on the pavement dangerous?
88910.e: On smooth ice your shoes hardly grip. You can easily slip and fall over.
88910.m: Ice on the pavement is very slippery.

88911.q: Where does a lake freeze first in winter?
a: In the middle of the water
Under the sand on the shore
88911.e: The cold air cools the water from above. That is why the layer of ice forms first on top of the lake.
88911.m: A lake freezes from the top.

88912.q: Why can fish survive under a frozen lake?
a: The water under the ice stays liquid
88912.e: Under the ice, the water stays liquid and a little warmer. There the fish can go on living.
88912.m: Under the ice, the water stays liquid.

88913.q: What are the white specks you often see in an ice cube?
88913.e: There is some air dissolved in water. When it freezes, this air gets trapped in the ice as tiny bubbles.
88913.m: White specks in ice are air bubbles.

88914.q: What do you need an ice scraper for in winter?
a: To remove ice from the car window
88914.e: After cold nights the car window is often covered in ice. You scrape it off with the ice scraper so you can see properly again.
88914.m: You clear ice off the car window with an ice scraper.

88915.q: How do you turn an open space into a natural ice rink in winter?
a: You spray water on it when it is freezing
88915.e: When it is freezing, you spray water onto the space in several thin layers. Each layer freezes until a smooth ice surface forms.
88915.m: For a natural ice rink, you spray water on in frosty weather.

88916.q: What does an ice pack do in a picnic bag?
88916.e: An ice pack is frozen in the freezer. In the bag it takes in heat and so keeps the food cool for longer.
88916.m: An ice pack keeps food cool.

88917.q: How does the ice of an artificial ice rink stay frozen even when it is above zero?
a: Cooling pipes lie under the ice
Lots of salt is scattered on it
88917.e: Under the surface of an artificial ice rink run pipes with a very cold liquid. They cool the ice from below.
88917.m: Cooling pipes keep the ice of an artificial rink frozen.

88918.q: What do you often hear when you put ice cubes into a warm drink?
88918.e: The outside of the ice cube suddenly gets warm while the inside stays cold. This creates fine cracks that crackle.
88918.m: Ice cubes crack in warm drinks.

88919.q: Why do you put ice cubes in a drink?
88919.e: The ice cubes take heat out of the drink. This makes the drink cooler.

88920.q: What colour is pure water in a glass?
88920.e: Pure water in a glass is colourless and see-through. You can look through it.

88921.q: How much of our body is made of water?
88921.e: An adult's body is more than half water. That is why we have to drink every day.
88921.m: Our body is more than half water.

88922.q: What happens when you pour water into a different bowl?
a: It takes the shape of the bowl
88922.e: Water is liquid and has no fixed shape. It fits any container.
88922.m: Water takes the shape of its container.

88923.q: What usually comes out of the tap when you turn it to the side marked red?
88923.e: On many mixer taps, red stands for hot and blue for cold water. That way you know which way to turn.
88923.m: Red on a tap stands for hot water.

88924.q: What happens to a dry sponge when you put it in water?
88924.e: A sponge has lots of small holes. The water gets in and fills them, so the sponge gets heavy and wet.

88925.q: About how much should schoolchildren drink each day?
88925.e: The Swiss Society for Nutrition recommends about one litre a day for children aged 6 to 12, ideally water or unsweetened tea. In hot weather and during sport you need more.
88925.m: Schoolchildren should drink about one litre a day.

88926.q: In which unit do you measure water in a measuring jug?
88926.e: A measuring jug shows litres, decilitres or millilitres. You use it to measure how much liquid is in it.
88926.m: In a measuring jug you measure water in litres.

88927.q: What does a sign saying “Not drinking water” on a fountain mean?
a: You should not drink from it
88927.e: Not all fountain water is checked and clean enough to drink. The sign warns you not to drink it.
88927.m: If it says “Not drinking water”, do not drink from the fountain.

88928.q: What state is water in at 20 degrees Celsius?
88928.e: At room temperature, water is neither frozen nor boiling. It is liquid.
88928.m: At room temperature, water is liquid.

88929.q: What can hot steam cause on the skin?
88929.e: Hot steam gives off a lot of heat to the skin. That can cause painful scalds.
88929.m: Hot steam can scald the skin.

88930.q: Where does warm steam from a pan go?
88930.e: Warm steam is lighter than the cooler air around it. That is why it rises.

88931.q: What do you use a steam iron for?
a: To get creases out of clothes
88931.e: The hot steam makes the fabric soft. Then you can smooth out the creases with the iron.

88932.q: How can you cook vegetables gently in the kitchen?
88932.e: When steaming, the vegetables sit above boiling water. The hot steam cooks them without them lying in the water.
88932.m: You can cook vegetables gently over steam.

88933.q: What whistles in the kitchen when the water in it boils?
88933.e: The steam flows through a small opening in the spout. This makes a loud whistling sound.
88933.m: A whistling kettle whistles when steam comes out.

88934.q: What forms in the sauna when you pour water onto the hot stones?
88934.e: On the very hot stones, the water turns into steam at once. This makes the air damp and it feels hotter.
88934.m: In the sauna, water on hot stones turns into steam.

88935.q: Why does the lid on a pan of boiling water sometimes rattle?
88935.e: Boiling water makes a lot of steam. It pushes against the lid from below and lifts it briefly again and again.
88935.m: Steam can lift a pan lid.

88936.q: What does a steam cleaner clean with?
88936.e: A steam cleaner heats water and blows the hot steam onto floors or tiles. The steam loosens the dirt.
88936.m: A steam cleaner cleans with hot steam.

88937.q: What does a coffee machine use to froth the milk?
88937.e: Hot steam streams into the milk from a thin tube. It warms the milk and blows air into it, which makes froth.

88938.q: What melts easily in a warm hand?
88938.e: Chocolate gets soft and runny even from the warmth of your hand. Stones, wood and glass, on the other hand, do not melt.
88938.m: Chocolate melts even in a warm hand.

88939.q: What do you melt in the caquelon for a fondue?
88939.e: For a cheese fondue, grated cheese is warmed in the caquelon until it is runny. Then you dip bread into it.
88939.m: For a fondue, you melt cheese.

88940.q: Why do you have to eat an ice cream quickly in summer?
88940.e: Ice cream is frozen. In the summer heat it quickly gets soft and drips.
88940.m: In summer an ice cream melts quickly.

88941.q: What quickly turns liquid in a hot frying pan?
88941.e: Butter is solid in the fridge. In the hot pan it quickly melts into a yellow liquid.
88941.m: Butter melts in a hot pan.

88942.q: What is often left when a snowman has melted in spring?
a: A puddle and the carrot nose
88942.e: The snow turns into water and forms a puddle. Carrots, stones or coal do not melt and are left lying there.
88942.m: A melted snowman leaves a puddle.

88943.q: What melts in a hot glue gun?
88943.e: In the hot glue gun, a plastic stick is heated. It melts and comes out at the front as liquid glue.
88943.m: In a hot glue gun, a glue stick melts.

88944.q: What is the Swiss dish called where cheese is melted by a heater and scraped off?
88944.e: For raclette, half a wheel of cheese or cheese in little pans is heated. The melted cheese is poured over potatoes.

88945.q: What happens to marshmallows that you toast over the fire?
88945.e: The heat makes the sugar in the marshmallow melt. That is why it gets soft and sticky inside.
88945.m: Over the fire, marshmallows get soft and sticky.

88946.q: What is it called when water turns into ice?
88946.e: When liquid water becomes solid, it freezes. This happens when it is cold enough.
88946.m: When water turns into ice, it freezes.

88947.q: What do you get if you freeze squash in small moulds with a stick?
88947.e: The squash goes solid in the freezer. That makes a home-made ice lolly.
88947.m: Frozen squash becomes an ice lolly.

88948.q: Where does the same amount of water freeze faster?
88948.e: In a flat dish the water is only a thin layer and has a lot of surface. So it gives off its heat faster.
88948.m: Water freezes faster in a flat dish.

88949.q: Why are strawberries often soft and mushy after thawing?
88949.e: When fruit freezes, sharp ice crystals form inside it. They damage the cells, which is why the strawberries go soft when they thaw.
88949.m: Ice crystals make thawed strawberries soft.

88950.q: Which freezes over faster on a cold night?
88950.e: A puddle has little water, so it cools down quickly. A lot of water, on the other hand, cools only slowly.
88950.m: A small puddle freezes over faster than a lake.

88951.q: Why does a fast-flowing stream rarely freeze over completely in winter?
88951.e: In fast-flowing water, a solid layer of ice can hardly form. Still water freezes much more easily.
88951.m: Flowing water freezes over less easily than still water.

88952.q: What happens to wet washing hung outside in a hard frost?
88952.e: The water in the fabric freezes into ice. That is why the washing goes hard and stiff as a board.
88952.m: Wet washing freezes stiff in a frost.

88953.q: What do the stars on a freezer compartment show?
88953.e: The more stars a freezer compartment has, the colder it gets inside. With four stars you can freeze food for a long time.
88953.m: The stars on a freezer show how cold it gets.

88954.q: What is the thin white coating of ice called that forms on meadows and car roofs on cold nights?
88954.e: In a frost, moisture from the air freezes directly onto cold surfaces. This makes a fine white coating of ice crystals.
88954.m: Hoar frost is a fine coating of ice from frosty nights.

88955.q: Why is a blackboard that has been wiped wet dry again after a while?
88955.e: The thin layer of water on the board slowly goes into the air as invisible vapour. Then the board is dry again.
88955.m: The water on the blackboard evaporates.

88956.q: Why can you soon smell perfume all over the room?
88956.e: Perfume evaporates easily. The scented particles spread through the air and reach our nose.
88956.m: Evaporating perfume spreads through the air.

88957.q: How do you stop the water in a glass from getting less over several days?
a: Put the glass in the sun
88957.e: A lid closes the glass. So the water cannot escape into the room air as vapour.

88958.q: Which evaporates faster, water or cooking oil?
88958.e: At room temperature, water evaporates slowly but steadily. Cooking oil, on the other hand, hardly evaporates and stays for a long time.
88958.m: Water evaporates much faster than cooking oil.

88959.q: Why should you always put the cap back on a glue stick or felt-tip pen?
a: Otherwise it gets lighter in colour
88959.e: Glue and felt-tip pens contain liquid. Without a cap, it evaporates and the pen dries out.
88959.m: Pens dry out without a cap.

88960.q: What happens to wet footprints on warm tiles at the swimming pool?
88960.e: The warm tiles give the water heat. So it evaporates quickly and the prints disappear.
88960.m: Wet footprints on warm tiles disappear quickly.

88961.q: Why do you have to top up the water in a paddling pool in summer?
a: Some of it evaporates in the sun
The pool soaks up the water
The water gets heavier in the sun
88961.e: In the sun, some water evaporates every day. Together with splashes, there is less and less in the pool.
88961.m: Water evaporates from the paddling pool in the sun.

88962.q: Where do wet shoes dry fastest?
88962.e: Warmth and fresh air make the water in the shoe evaporate faster. In a bag, the moisture cannot escape.
88962.m: Wet shoes dry fastest somewhere warm and airy.

88963.q: Why does the bathroom mirror steam up after a shower?
88963.e: When you shower, a lot of water vapour gets into the air. On the cool mirror it turns back into tiny droplets.
88963.m: On the cool mirror, water vapour turns into droplets.

88964.q: What helps against a steamed-up car windscreen?
88964.e: The ventilation blows air onto the windscreen. This makes the droplets disappear and you can see clearly again.
88964.m: The ventilation clears a steamed-up windscreen.

88965.q: What happens to the mist on the bathroom mirror after a while?
88965.e: When the air gets drier, the tiny droplets evaporate again. Then the mirror is clear again.
88965.m: The mist on the mirror disappears over time.

88966.q: Where do drops collect on a pan lid while cooking?
88966.e: The steam from the pan rises to the lid. On its underside it cools down and turns into drops.
88966.m: Drops collect under the pan lid.

88967.q: Why do little icicles often hang from branches and fences after freezing rain?
88967.e: With freezing rain, rain falls on very cold branches and fences. As it drips off, it freezes at once into little icicles.
88967.m: After freezing rain, icicles hang from branches.

88968.q: What do you often see at the back of a car's exhaust on cold days?
88968.e: The exhaust gases contain water vapour. In the cold air it turns into tiny droplets and you see little white clouds.
88968.m: In winter you see little white clouds at the exhaust.

88969.q: What do you often find as droplets on the grass after a cool, clear night?
88969.e: At night the grass cools down a lot. Moisture from the air settles on it as fine droplets; this is called dew.
88969.m: Dewdrops form on the grass on cool nights.

88970.q: Why do some people breathe on their glasses before cleaning them?
a: The breath makes the glass slightly damp
The breath makes the glass hot
The breath makes the glass harder
88970.e: Warm breath contains water vapour. On the cooler glass it forms a damp film that makes smudges easier to wipe off.
88970.m: Glasses you have breathed on are easier to clean.

88971.q: How fast do snowflakes fall compared with raindrops?
a: They do not fall at all
88971.e: Snowflakes are light and have lots of little arms. The air slows them down a lot, so they float down slowly.
88971.m: Snowflakes fall more slowly than raindrops.

88972.q: What is trapped between the flakes of a fresh layer of snow?
88972.e: Fresh snow is loose and is mostly made of air. That is why it is so light and soft.

88973.q: What is snow called that the wind blows together into high heaps?
88973.e: Strong wind carries the snow along and drops it behind obstacles. This makes high snowdrifts.
88973.m: The wind can pile snow up into drifts.

88974.q: What do you call freshly fallen snow?
88974.e: Snow that has only just fallen is called new snow. It is loose and soft.
88974.m: Freshly fallen snow is called new snow.

88975.q: What is a good thing to look at snowflakes on before they melt?
a: The warm palm of your hand
88975.e: On cold, dark fabric, the flakes do not melt at once and stand out well. So you can see their delicate shapes.
88975.m: You can see snowflakes well on a cold, dark glove.

88976.q: What do you use to clear snow from the pavement in front of the house?
88976.e: With the wide snow shovel you push the snow aside. So the path is clear again.
88976.m: You clear snow with a snow shovel.

88977.q: What happens to a snowflake that lands on your warm hand?
a: It stays there for a long time
88977.e: Your hand is warm. This quickly turns the little snowflake into a drop of water.
88977.m: A snowflake melts on a warm hand.

88978.q: Why do skiers like to wear ski goggles when it is snowing?
a: So no flakes fly into their eyes
88978.e: When it snows and you are moving fast, flakes fly into your face. Ski goggles protect your eyes and you see better.
88978.m: Ski goggles protect your eyes from snowflakes.

88979.q: Where do icicles often hang on village fountains in winter?
a: On the bottom of the trough
In the water of the trough
88979.e: Water constantly splashes and drips from the fountain spout. In a frost it freezes into icicles there.
88979.m: Icicles often form on the fountain spout.

88980.q: Why should you not suck icicles from the roof?
88980.e: The meltwater flows over the roof and picks up dirt. This dirt then ends up in the icicle too.
88980.m: Icicles from the roof can be dirty.

88981.q: What do icicles and stalactites have in common?
88981.e: With both, water drips down and leaves something behind. With an icicle it is freezing water, with a stalactite it is limestone.
88981.m: Icicles and stalactites grow from drips.

88982.q: What do you often see at the tip of a growing icicle?
88982.e: The water runs down the icicle and collects at the tip. A drop often hangs there before it freezes or falls.
88982.m: A drop often hangs at the tip of an icicle.

88983.q: How long can icicles on roofs get?
88983.e: In long cold spells with lots of meltwater, icicles keep growing. Some get longer than a metre.
88983.m: Icicles can be more than a metre long.

88984.q: What is often left when a muddy puddle has dried up?
88984.e: The water disappears, but the soil in it stays behind. It dries into a cracked layer of mud.
88984.m: Dried-up puddles leave dry mud behind.

88985.q: What is best to wear for jumping in puddles?
88985.e: Wellies are tall and watertight. So your feet stay dry when you jump in puddles.
88985.m: You wear wellies for jumping in puddles.

88986.q: What do you hear when you jump into a puddle?
88986.e: When you jump, the water is suddenly pushed away and splashes up. This makes a splashing sound.
88986.m: Jumping in a puddle goes splash.

88987.q: What do birds often do at a puddle?
88987.e: For many birds, a puddle is a little bath and a place to drink. They drink from it and clean their feathers.
88987.m: Birds like to bathe and drink at puddles.

88988.q: What do you call a small, still pool of water in the woods that is bigger than a puddle?
88988.e: A pond like this is a small, shallow body of water. It can dry up in summer and is important for frogs and newts.
88988.m: A pond is a small, still body of water.

88989.q: Why should you ride slowly through a big puddle on your bike?
a: You cannot see how deep it is
88989.e: A hole or a stone may be hidden under the water. If you ride slowly, you are less likely to fall.

88990.q: Why does it splash when a car drives through a puddle?
a: The wheels push the water away
The water is as light as air
88990.e: The heavy wheels push the water quickly aside. It splashes up, which is why you keep your distance at the roadside.
88990.m: Car wheels push puddle water aside.

88991.q: Why are there often especially many puddles after a thunderstorm?
a: A lot of rain falls in a short time
88991.e: In thunderstorms, a lot of rain often falls at once. The ground cannot soak up so much water quickly enough.
88991.m: Heavy storm rain makes lots of puddles.

88992.q: What do you see when water is boiling hard in a pan?
88992.e: At the hot bottom of the pan, water turns into steam. The steam bubbles rise and make the water bubble.
88992.m: Boiling water bubbles with big bubbles.

88993.q: What does a kettle do as soon as the water boils?
88993.e: A kettle has a switch inside that reacts to the steam. When the water boils, the appliance switches off.
88993.m: A kettle switches itself off when the water boils.

88994.q: Why do you turn the pan handle inwards when cooking?
a: So nobody pulls the pan down
88994.e: A handle sticking out over the edge of the cooker can easily be knocked. Then hot water could fall down and scald someone.
88994.m: For safety, turn pan handles inwards.

88995.q: What happens to pasta in boiling water?
88995.e: The hard, dry pasta takes up water in the hot water. As it does, it gets soft and bigger.
88995.m: Pasta gets soft in boiling water.

88996.q: What can happen if a pan of boiling water is too full?
88996.e: The rising bubbles lift the water. If the pan is too full, it runs over the edge.
88996.m: A pan that is too full boils over.

88997.q: What happens to water that you leave boiling for a very long time?
88997.e: While it boils, water keeps turning into steam and escaping. If you let it boil too long, the pan is empty at some point.
88997.m: Boiling water gets less over time.

88998.q: What do you do if the water in the pan is bubbling too hard?
a: Put ice cubes on the cooker
88998.e: With less heat, fewer steam bubbles form. The water then boils more gently and does not splash.
88998.m: If it bubbles too hard, turn the heat down.

88999.q: Why should you not pour boiling water into a thin, cold glass?
88999.e: The glass suddenly gets hot inside while staying cold outside. This can make it crack and shatter.
88999.m: Boiling water can crack a cold glass.

89000.q: What do you hear just before the water in a kettle boils?
89000.e: Steam bubbles form at the hot bottom and collapse again at first. This makes a rushing sound.
89000.m: Just before boiling, the water makes a rushing sound.

89001.e: The sun warms the air. Then the droplets evaporate and the fog disappears.
89001.m: The sun can clear the fog.

89002.q: What do ships use to warn each other in thick fog?
89002.e: A foghorn makes a very loud, deep sound. So other ships can hear where you are, even if they cannot see anything.
89002.m: In fog, ships warn each other with a foghorn.

89003.q: What makes a spider's web easy to see on a foggy morning?
89003.e: The tiny droplets from the fog settle on the threads. Then the whole web glistens.
89003.m: Fog droplets make spiders' webs visible.

89004.q: What is sometimes difficult at an airport in very thick fog?
89004.e: In thick fog, pilots find it hard to see the runway. That is why there are sometimes delays.
89004.m: Thick fog makes take-offs and landings harder.

89005.q: Which lights on a car are specially meant for fog?
89005.e: Front fog lights sit low on the car and shine widely onto the road. At the back, a bright red rear fog light makes the car easier to see.

89006.q: What is very light, thin fog called that you can still see quite far through?
89006.e: Haze is like a fine veil in the air. It is much less dense than real fog.
89006.m: Haze is a thin, light fog.

89007.q: Where does fog often form in the morning?
89007.e: The air over water is especially damp. When it cools down at night, patches of fog often form there.
89007.m: Fog often forms over lakes and rivers.

89008.q: What should drivers do with the distance to the car in front when it is foggy?
89008.e: In fog you spot obstacles late. With more distance there is enough time to brake.

89010.q: Which present-day country did Johannes Kepler come from?
89010.e: Kepler was born in 1571 in Weil der Stadt in what is now Baden-Württemberg. Later he worked in Graz, Prague and Linz.

89011.q: What does Kepler's second law (the law of areas) say?
a: The line from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times
Large planets move more slowly than small ones
89011.e: The imaginary line from the Sun to the planet sweeps out equal areas in equal lengths of time. Kepler found this law of areas by carefully analysing observations.
89011.m: According to Kepler, equal times mean equal areas.

89012.q: Which quantities does Kepler's third law link?
89012.e: The square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis. That is why planets further away take much longer for one orbit.
89012.m: The further a planet is from the Sun, the longer its orbit takes.

89014.q: Whose precise observations did Johannes Kepler use for his laws?
89014.e: In Prague, Kepler worked with the very precise measurements of the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe. He worked out his laws from them.
89014.m: Kepler built on the measurements of Tycho Brahe.

89015.e: Kepler was a mathematician and astronomer. Among other things he worked for the emperor in Prague and found the laws of planetary motion.
89015.m: Johannes Kepler was an astronomer and mathematician.

89016.q: Which Italian scientist did Kepler exchange letters with about the telescope?
89016.e: In 1610 Kepler read Galileo's report on his discoveries with the telescope and replied with a work of his own. The two were in contact by letter.
89016.m: Kepler and Galileo exchanged ideas about the telescope.

89017.q: Strictly speaking, around which point do the Earth and the Moon orbit together?
a: Around their common centre of gravity
Around the centre of the Moon
Around the point halfway between them
89017.e: The Earth and the Moon both orbit their common centre of gravity. Because the Earth has much more mass, this point is still inside the Earth, around 4700 km from the Earth's centre.
89017.m: The Earth and the Moon orbit a common centre of gravity.

89018.q: Why does a satellite in orbit not fall onto the Earth?
a: It is always falling, but moves sideways so fast that it misses the Earth
There is no gravity in space
Engines keep holding it up all the time
The air carries it like an aeroplane
89018.e: Gravity acts in orbit too. But the satellite is so fast that the Earth's surface curves away beneath it while it falls.
89018.m: A satellite keeps falling around the Earth.

89019.q: Roughly how fast must a satellite in low Earth orbit be?
89019.e: For a circular orbit just above the Earth you need about 7.9 km per second. This is called the first cosmic velocity.
89019.m: For a low Earth orbit you need almost eight kilometres per second.

89020.q: Which satellites help a mobile phone find its own location?
89020.e: Navigation satellites such as GPS or Galileo constantly send time signals. From several signals the phone works out where it is.
89020.m: Navigation satellites show the phone where it is.

89021.q: What is the orbit called of a satellite that seems to stand still over the same point on the equator?
89021.e: In geostationary orbit, one orbit takes exactly as long as one turn of the Earth. That is why the satellite seems to stand still over one point.
89021.m: Geostationary satellites seem to stand still over one point.

89022.q: What slowly slows down satellites in very low orbits?
a: The magnetic fields of the planets
89022.e: Even a few hundred kilometres up there is still very thin air. It slows satellites down, so without a boost they sink and finally burn up.
89022.m: The thin remaining air slows down low satellites.

89023.q: Roughly how great is the average distance between the Earth and the Moon?
89023.e: The Moon orbits the Earth at an average distance of about 384,400 km. That is around 30 Earth diameters.
89023.m: On average the Moon is about 384,000 kilometres from the Earth.

89024.q: Roughly how great is the escape velocity at the Earth's surface?
89024.e: Without propulsion, a body at the Earth's surface must be about 11.2 km/s fast to escape the Earth's gravity completely. Air resistance is left out here.
89024.m: To leave the Earth completely you need over eleven kilometres per second.

89025.q: What does the term “escape velocity” mean?
a: The minimum speed needed to escape a body in space without further propulsion
The top speed of a spacecraft
The speed at which a planet travels round the Sun
89025.e: At escape velocity, a body has enough energy of motion to overcome the pull of a body in space. After that it does not come back.
89025.m: Whatever reaches escape velocity does not come back.

89026.q: Roughly how great is the escape velocity on the Moon?
89026.e: The Moon has much less mass than the Earth. So about 2.4 km/s is enough to leave it.
89026.m: It is much easier to get away from the Moon than from the Earth.

89027.q: A rocket is slower than escape velocity and switches off its engine. What happens?
a: It falls back or orbits the Earth
It flies out into space for ever
It stays still in the air
It flies straight to the Sun
89027.e: If a rocket is too slow, the Earth's gravity pulls it back. But with enough speed it can stay in an orbit.
89027.m: Anything slower than escape velocity cannot break free of the Earth completely.

89028.q: Why must a probe be faster to leave the whole solar system than just to get away from the Earth?
a: The Sun holds on to it with its gravity too
There is air resistance in space
The other planets blow it back
Sunlight slows it down a lot
89028.e: Whatever escapes the Earth is still in the grip of the Sun. To leave the solar system, you need around 16.7 km/s starting from the Earth.
89028.m: To leave the solar system you also have to escape the Sun.

89029.q: Does escape velocity depend on the mass of the rocket?
a: No, it is the same for light and heavy bodies
Only for rockets made of metal
89029.e: Escape velocity depends only on the mass and the radius of the body in space. A heavy rocket needs more energy, but the same speed.
89029.m: Escape velocity is the same for a pebble and a rocket.

89030.q: For which bodies in space is the escape velocity greater than the speed of light?
89030.e: With a black hole you would have to be faster than light to escape. That is why not even light can leave a black hole.
89030.m: Not even light escapes from a black hole.

89031.q: Which planet in our solar system has the greatest escape velocity?
89031.e: Jupiter is the most massive planet. Its escape velocity is around 60 km/s.
89031.m: The giant Jupiter holds on most strongly.

89032.q: Above which line on the Earth are all geostationary satellites?
89032.e: A satellite can only seem to stand still above the equator. On a tilted orbit it would swing north and south across the sky.
89032.m: Geostationary satellites are always above the equator.

89033.q: Roughly how long does one orbit of a geostationary satellite round the Earth take?
89033.e: The satellite circles the Earth exactly as fast as the Earth spins on its axis. That takes just under 24 hours.
89033.m: A geostationary satellite takes as long for one lap as the Earth takes for one turn.

89034.q: Why do you not have to keep turning a satellite dish for television?
a: The geostationary satellite stands still as seen from the Earth
The dish receives from all directions
The satellite only broadcasts at night
89034.e: A geostationary satellite moves in step with the Earth. Seen from below, it always stays at the same point in the sky.
89034.m: A satellite dish always points at the same point in the sky.

89035.q: Which direction do satellite dishes in Switzerland usually point?
89035.e: The geostationary satellites are above the equator, so seen from Switzerland they are in the south. That is why the dishes point up at an angle towards the south.
89035.m: In Switzerland satellite dishes face south.

89036.q: What are many satellites in geostationary orbit used for?
a: For television, radio and weather pictures
89036.e: Because these satellites always stay above the same place, they are good for television, telephone and weather watching. The writer Arthur C. Clarke made the idea well known in 1945.
89036.m: Geostationary satellites broadcast television and watch the weather.

89037.q: Which European weather satellites are in geostationary orbit?
89037.e: From geostationary orbit, the Meteosat satellites constantly send pictures of Europe and Africa. They are also used for weather forecasts in Switzerland.
89037.m: Meteosat watches Europe's weather from a fixed point.

89038.q: In which direction does a geostationary satellite move round the Earth?
a: From west to east, as the Earth spins
It does not move at all
89038.e: It has to move in the same direction as the Earth's spin, that is, eastwards. Only then does it stay above the same place.
89038.m: A geostationary satellite orbits in the direction of the Earth's spin.

89039.q: Where on Earth can geostationary satellites not be received?
89039.e: From the polar regions, the satellites above the equator are below the horizon. Other satellite systems are needed there.
89039.m: At the poles, geostationary satellites are hidden behind the horizon.

89040.q: Roughly how strong is the Sun's tidal effect on the Earth compared with the Moon's?
89040.e: The Sun has much more mass, but it is around 400 times further away. Because the tidal force decreases very sharply with distance, it reaches only about half of the Moon's effect.
89040.m: The Sun produces tides about half as strong as the Moon's.

89041.q: Roughly how many high tides are there per day on most coasts?
89041.e: The tidal force creates two tidal bulges: one on the side facing the Moon and one on the side facing away. That is why high tide comes about every 12 hours and 25 minutes.
89041.m: On most coasts high tide comes twice a day.

89042.q: When does an especially high spring tide occur?
a: At new moon and full moon
89042.e: At new moon and full moon, the Sun, the Earth and the Moon are in a line. Their tidal forces add up.
89042.m: At new moon and full moon there are spring tides.

89043.q: What is an especially weak tide called, when the Sun and the Moon are at right angles to the Earth?
89043.e: At half moon, the tidal forces of the Sun and the Moon work against each other. The difference between low and high tide is then small.
89043.m: At half moon there is only a weak neap tide.

89044.q: Why is there also a tidal bulge on the side of the Earth facing away from the Moon?
a: The Moon pulls more weakly there than at the Earth's centre
The Sun shines more strongly there
89044.e: The Moon's pull decreases with distance. On the far side, the water therefore lags a little behind the Earth and forms a second tidal bulge.
89044.m: The tidal force creates tidal bulges on both sides of the Earth.

89045.q: Why do low and high tide shift by around 50 minutes from day to day?
a: The Moon moves on along its orbit
The Earth spins more slowly every day
The Sun rises later every day
The sea water flows more and more slowly
89045.e: It takes about 24 hours and 50 minutes until the same place is under the Moon again, because the Moon has moved on in the meantime. That is why the tides come later every day.
89045.m: The tides follow the Moon and come a little later each day.

89046.q: How does the distance between the Moon and the Earth change because of the tides?
a: It gets about 3.8 cm bigger every year
It gets about 3.8 m smaller every year
It always stays exactly the same
It gets about 38 km bigger every year
89046.e: Through the tidal effect, the Moon gets momentum from the Earth and slowly moves away. This is measured with laser beams aimed at mirrors on the Moon.
89046.m: The Moon moves almost four centimetres further away every year.

89047.q: Why do you not notice any tides on Lake Geneva or Lake Constance?
a: The lakes are far too small for that
The Moon does not shine there
The Moon does not attract fresh water
89047.e: The tidal force acts on lakes too, but in a small lake the water rises by only a few millimetres. Only in large oceans are there differences of several metres.
89047.m: Noticeable tides only happen in large seas.

89048.q: Roughly how long does one complete precession cycle of the Earth's axis take?
89048.e: The Earth's axis slowly traces out a cone, like a spinning top. One lap takes about 25,800 years and is called a Platonic year.
89048.m: The Earth's axis wobbles round once in around 26,000 years.

89049.q: What causes the precession of the Earth's axis?
a: The pull of the Sun and the Moon on the bulge at the equator
The movement of the oceans alone
89049.e: The Earth is a little fatter at the equator. The Sun and the Moon pull on this bulge and try to straighten the axis, which makes it swerve aside like a spinning top.
89049.m: The Sun and the Moon pull on the Earth's fat middle.

89050.q: Will the Pole Star stay our pole star for ever, given precession?
a: No, over time the Earth's axis points at other stars
Yes, it stays fixed for ever
Yes, as long as the Sun shines
No, it will go out next year
89050.e: The Earth's axis slowly moves round in a circle. So in many thousands of years it will point at other stars, for example the bright star Vega.
89050.m: The Pole Star will not be the pole star for ever.

89051.q: How fast does the direction of the Earth's axis change because of precession?
a: Very slowly, you only notice it over centuries
All the way round once a year
89051.e: A whole lap takes around 26,000 years. That is why even ancient astronomers only noticed the shift by comparing old measurements with new ones.
89051.m: Precession is a very slow movement.

89052.q: With which toy can you watch precession well?
89052.e: A spinning top that is tilted does not fall over; instead its axis slowly moves round in a circle. This exact movement is called precession.
89052.m: A tilted spinning top shows precession.

89053.q: At the start of spring the Sun is now in front of a different constellation from 2000 years ago. Why?
a: The Earth's axis slowly changes its direction
89053.e: Because of precession, the point where the Sun stands at the start of spring moves slowly through the constellations of the zodiac.
89053.m: Precession moves the start of spring through the zodiac.

89054.q: What mainly changes because of the precession of the Earth's axis?
a: The direction the axis points in
The length of a day by hours
89054.e: The tilt of the Earth's axis stays at about 23.4 degrees. But the direction in space in which it points changes.
89054.m: With precession, the direction of the Earth's axis turns.

89055.q: Which famous physicist was able to explain why Mercury's orbit slowly turns?
89055.e: Mercury's orbit turns slightly faster than Newton's law would lead you to expect. Einstein explained this in 1915 with his theory of relativity.
89055.m: Einstein's theory of relativity explains the turning of Mercury's orbit.

89056.q: Why do we need leap years?
a: A solar year lasts around 365 days and almost 6 hours
The Earth spins more slowly every four years
The Moon needs an extra day
Otherwise February is too short for winter
89056.e: A tropical year lasts about 365.2422 days. Without leap days, the calendar would drift out of step with the seasons.
89056.m: Leap days keep the calendar in step with the seasons.

89057.q: Which day is added in a leap year?
89057.e: In a leap year February has 29 days instead of 28. The year then has 366 days.
89057.m: In a leap year February has 29 days.

a: No, because it can be divided by 100 but not by 400
Yes, because it can be divided by 4
Yes, every century year is one
No, because it is an odd number
89058.e: Century years are only leap years if they can be divided by 400. 1900 cannot, but 2000 can.
89058.m: Whole centuries are only leap years if they can be divided by 400.

89059.q: In the calendar reform of 1582, which day came straight after Thursday 4 October?
89059.e: To bring the calendar back in line with the seasons, ten days were left out. So 4 October 1582 was followed directly by 15 October.
89059.m: In the calendar reform of 1582, ten days were skipped.

89060.q: Which pope introduced the Gregorian calendar with today's leap year rule in 1582?
89060.e: Pope Gregory XIII had the calendar reformed in 1582. The rule for century years was introduced at the same time.
89060.m: The Gregorian calendar is named after Pope Gregory XIII.

89061.q: Who introduced a calendar with a leap day every four years in 45 BC?
89061.e: Julius Caesar's Julian calendar added a leap day every four years. This made it slightly too long, which Gregory XIII later corrected.
89061.m: The Julian calendar goes back to Julius Caesar.

89062.q: Why were there two different calendars in the Swiss Confederation for a long time?
a: Catholic and Protestant areas switched at different times
Every canton had its own days of the week
A different calendar applied in winter
89062.e: Most Catholic areas adopted the new calendar in 1584, but most Protestant ones only in 1701. In the Grisons it took until 1812.
89062.m: In Switzerland two different calendars were in use for a long time.

89063.q: How many leap years are there from 2001 up to and including 2100?
89063.e: The leap years are 2004, 2008 and so on up to 2096, which makes 96 ÷ 4 = 24 years. 2100 can be divided by 100 but not by 400, so it is not a leap year.
89063.m: There are 24 leap years in the 21st century.

89064.q: What is the next leap year after 2026?
89064.e: Leap years can be divided by 4. 2028 ÷ 4 = 507, so 2028 is the next leap year.
89064.m: The next leap year after 2026 is 2028.

89065.q: By how much does the local time of two places one degree of longitude apart differ?
89065.e: The Earth turns through 360 degrees in 24 hours. So for 1 degree it needs 24 × 60 ÷ 360 = 4 minutes.
89065.m: One degree of longitude makes four minutes of local time.

89066.q: How long is a mean solar day?
89066.e: The mean solar day is the time from noon to noon, averaged over the year. Our clocks are set by it.
89066.m: Our clocks count mean solar days of 24 hours.

89067.q: Why is a solar day longer than a sidereal day?
a: The Earth moves on along its orbit round the Sun
The Sun goes round the Earth
The Moon slows the Earth down every day
The stars move faster than the Sun
89067.e: During one turn, the Earth moves a little way along its orbit. So it has to turn a bit more until the Sun is in the south again.
89067.m: Because of its orbit, the Earth has to turn a bit further for a solar day.

89068.q: How many sidereal days does a year have compared with solar days?
89068.e: A year has around 365.24 solar days, but around 366.24 sidereal days. The orbit round the Sun “costs” exactly one turn.
89068.m: A year has one more sidereal day than solar days.

89069.q: Roughly how much earlier does a particular star rise each night?
89069.e: Because the sidereal day is about 4 minutes shorter, the stars appear a little earlier every evening. That is why you see different constellations depending on the season.
89069.m: The stars rise about four minutes earlier every day.

89070.q: What time does a sundial show?
a: The true local time by the position of the Sun
89070.e: A sundial follows the actual position of the Sun at that place. So it can differ from mean solar time by up to about a quarter of an hour.
89070.m: A sundial shows the true solar time of the place.

89071.q: Over the year, by how much at most can a sundial differ from steady clock time?
a: By about a quarter of an hour
89071.e: The Sun is not in the south at exactly the same clock time every day. So over the year a sundial is up to about 16 minutes fast or slow.
89071.m: Sundials differ by up to a quarter of an hour.

89072.q: Roughly how far is Saturn from the Sun?
89072.e: Saturn orbits the Sun at a distance of around 9.5 AU. So it is almost ten times as far from the Sun as the Earth.
89072.m: Saturn is almost ten astronomical units from the Sun.

89073.q: Roughly what distance is one astronomical unit?
a: The average distance between the Earth and the Sun
The distance between the Earth and the Moon
The diameter of the Milky Way
The distance to the nearest star
89073.e: The astronomical unit was based on the distance from the Earth to the Sun. It is well suited to distances in the solar system.
89073.m: The astronomical unit is the distance from the Earth to the Sun.

89074.q: Uranus is around 19 AU from the Sun. Roughly how long does sunlight take to reach it?
89074.e: For 1 AU, light needs just over 8 minutes (around 8.3 minutes). For 19 AU that is about 19 × 8.3 ≈ 160 minutes, so around 2 hours 40 minutes.
89074.m: Sunlight takes over two and a half hours to reach Uranus.

89075.q: Roughly how far is Jupiter from the Sun?
89075.e: Jupiter orbits the Sun at a distance of around 5.2 AU. So it is just over five times as far from the Sun as the Earth.
89075.m: Jupiter is around five astronomical units from the Sun.

89076.q: Roughly how far is Neptune from the Sun?
89076.e: Neptune is the outermost planet. It orbits the Sun at a distance of about 30 AU.
89076.m: Neptune is around thirty astronomical units from the Sun.

89077.q: What do astronomers mainly use the astronomical unit for?
a: For distances in the solar system
89077.e: One astronomical unit is around 150 million kilometres, the distance from the Earth to the Sun. It makes it easy to compare the distances of the planets.
89077.m: The astronomical unit is used to measure distances in the solar system.

89079.q: Roughly how many kilometres are 2 astronomical units?
89079.e: One AU is around 150 million km. So two AU are 2 × 150 million km = 300 million km.
89079.m: Two astronomical units are about 300 million kilometres.

89080.q: What is the point of a planet's orbit closest to the Sun called?
89080.e: “Peri” means “near” in Greek, and “Helios” is the Sun. At perihelion a planet is closest to the Sun.
89080.m: At perihelion a planet is closest to the Sun.

89081.q: What is the point of a planet's orbit furthest from the Sun called?
89081.e: “Apo” means “away from” in Greek. At aphelion a planet is furthest from the Sun.
89081.m: At aphelion a planet is furthest from the Sun.

89082.q: In which month is the Earth furthest from the Sun?
89082.e: The Earth reaches its aphelion at the beginning of July. Even so, it is summer here then.
89082.m: At the beginning of July the Earth is furthest from the Sun.

89083.q: Roughly how much does the Earth's distance from the Sun change over a year?
89083.e: The Earth's orbit is almost a circle. So the distance to the Sun varies by only just over 3 per cent, far too little to explain the seasons.
89083.m: The distance between the Earth and the Sun changes only a little during the year.

89084.q: Roughly how great is the distance between the Earth and the Sun at perihelion?
89084.e: At perihelion the Earth is about 147.1 million km from the Sun, at aphelion about 152.1 million km. So the orbit is almost circular.
89084.m: The Earth's orbit is only slightly elliptical.

89085.q: When does the Earth move fastest along its orbit?
89085.e: Close to the Sun, the Earth is fastest at just over 30 km/s. At the point furthest from the Sun it is only around 29 km/s.
89085.m: Close to the Sun the Earth travels fastest.

89086.q: What is a full moon called when the Moon is especially close to the Earth?
89086.e: The Moon's orbit is not quite round. If the Moon is especially close at full moon, it looks a bit bigger and brighter. This is called a supermoon.
89086.m: A supermoon is a full moon close to the Earth.

89089.q: How does the force of attraction change if the mass of one of the two bodies is doubled?
89089.e: The gravitational force is proportional to the product of the two masses. Double the mass of one body gives double the force.

89091.q: According to a well-known story, which fruit is said to have made Newton think about gravity?
89091.e: Newton later said that a falling apple had got him thinking. He wondered whether the same force also keeps the Moon in its orbit.
89091.m: A falling apple is said to have led Newton to gravity.

89092.q: On which body in space would you be heavier than on Earth?
89092.e: Jupiter has over 300 times as much mass as the Earth. At the top of its clouds, gravity is about 2.5 times as strong as here.
89092.m: On Jupiter you would be around two and a half times as heavy.

89094.q: Which planet has the shortest orbital period round the Sun?
89094.e: Mercury is the planet closest to the Sun and needs only about 88 days for one orbit. So a year on Mercury is shorter than a quarter of a year on Earth.
89094.m: Mercury goes round the Sun in only 88 days.

89095.q: Why does a year on Neptune last much longer than a year on Earth?
a: Neptune is much further from the Sun
Neptune spins faster on its axis
Neptune is smaller than the Earth
89095.e: The further a planet is from the Sun, the longer its path and the more slowly it orbits. Neptune takes around 165 Earth years for one lap.
89095.m: Distant planets take a very long time to go round the Sun.

89096.q: Roughly how long does Jupiter take for one orbit of the Sun?
89096.e: Jupiter takes about 11.9 Earth years for one lap round the Sun. So it moves on by roughly one zodiac constellation each year.
89096.m: Jupiter orbits the Sun in around twelve years.

89097.q: Roughly how long is a year on Mars?
89097.e: Mars is further from the Sun than the Earth and takes about 687 days for one orbit. That is just under two Earth years.
89097.m: A year on Mars lasts almost two Earth years.

89098.q: Roughly how long does Saturn take for one orbit of the Sun?
89098.e: Saturn is the sixth planet from the Sun. It takes around 29.5 Earth years for one lap.
89098.m: A year on Saturn lasts almost thirty Earth years.

89099.q: Roughly how long does Venus take for one orbit of the Sun?
89099.e: Venus is the second planet from the Sun. It takes about 225 Earth days for one lap.
89099.m: A year on Venus lasts around 225 Earth days.

89100.q: Which planet takes the longest for one orbit of the Sun?
89100.e: Neptune is the outermost planet in our solar system. It takes around 165 Earth years for one lap, Uranus around 84.
89100.m: The outermost planet, Neptune, has the longest year.

89101.q: What does a planet's orbital period mean?
a: The time for one whole lap round the Sun
The time for one turn on its axis
The time until the Sun's light arrives
The time from sunrise to sunset
89101.e: The orbital period is the length of one full lap round the Sun, that is, the planet's year. Turning on its axis, on the other hand, gives the day.
89101.m: The orbital period is a planet's year.

89102.q: In which unit, named after Isaac Newton, are forces such as weight measured?
89102.e: The unit of force is called the newton (N). On Earth, a body with a mass of 1 kg has a weight of just under 10 N.

89103.q: According to Newton's law of gravitation, between which bodies is there a force of attraction?
89103.e: According to Newton, all bodies with mass attract each other, even two apples. But with small masses this force is tiny.
89103.m: All bodies with mass attract each other.

89104.q: What shape is the Earth's orbit round the Sun?
89104.e: The Earth's orbit is a slightly stretched ellipse. That is why there is a point closest to the Sun, the perihelion, and a point furthest from the Sun, the aphelion.
89104.m: The Earth's orbit is an almost circular ellipse.

89105.q: What is the time called that is based on the Earth's turning relative to the stars?
89105.e: Sidereal time is based on the sidereal day. Astronomers use it to know which stars are in the south at that moment.
89105.m: Astronomers point their telescopes using sidereal time.

89106.q: Roughly how far is Venus from the Sun?
89106.e: Venus orbits the Sun at a distance of around 0.72 AU. So it is closer to the Sun than the Earth.
89106.m: Venus is around 0.7 astronomical units from the Sun.

89107.q: What does a satellite need to move from its orbit to a higher one?
a: More sunlight on its solar panels
89107.e: Without propulsion, a satellite stays in its orbit. To climb higher, it has to speed up with its engine.
89107.m: A satellite needs thrust for a higher orbit.

89108.q: What is the difference in height between high water and low water called?
89108.e: The tidal range tells you how much the water rises and falls between low and high tide. On many North Sea coasts it is several metres.
89108.m: The tidal range measures the difference between low and high tide.

89109.q: Which small mountain lake is traditionally seen as the source of the Rhine?
89109.e: Lake Toma (Lai da Tuma in Romansh) is a small mountain lake at the very top of the Surselva. It has long been seen as the source of the Vorderrhein and so of the Rhine.
89109.m: Lake Toma is seen as the source of the Rhine.

89110.q: In which canton is Lake Toma, the source of the Rhine?
89110.e: Lake Toma lies at the top of the Vorderrhein valley in the municipality of Tujetsch in the Grisons. The village of Sedrun also belongs to Tujetsch.
89110.m: The source of the Rhine is in the Grisons.
